deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page develops elementary divisibility theory from the Euclidean algorithm. It proves that if a and b are coprime, then aK and b have the same common divisors as K and b. Two special cases are drawn from this. (i) A product of numbers each coprime to v is coprime to v. (ii) If b divides aK with gcd(a,b)=1, then b divides K; this is Euclid's lemma.

This page states the next standard corollary. 'If a number is divisible by several others which are all relatively prime, i.e. each to each, then it is also divisible by their product.' In modern terms: if b | a, c | a, d | a and gcd(b,c)=gcd(b,d)=gcd(c,d)=1, then bcd | a.

Riemann writes 'a | b, c, d' to mean 'a is divisible by b, c, d'. The bar here is a separator or shorthand and reads opposite to the modern 'b | a' convention.

Proof sketch on the page:
1. Since b divides a, write a = m b.
2. Since c divides a = m b and gcd(b,c)=1, Euclid's lemma (case (ii) of the previous page) gives c | m. So m = n c ('folglich m = nc').
3. Hence a = n b c (the last line reads roughly 'a = nc·b'). This gives bc | a.

Implicit continuation (mine, not written on the page): by case (i), bc is coprime to d. Since d divides a = n(bc), Euclid's lemma again gives d | n, so bcd | a. Induction extends this to any finite pairwise-coprime family.

The page is a fragment of an elementary exposition of number theory, probably lecture or teaching notes. It stops after the two-factor step.
errors: No mathematical error. The proof is left incomplete: only the step to bc | a is written. The extension to d (using that bc is coprime to d, from the previous page's first special case) is not carried out.
Pairwise coprimality is actually more than needed. It suffices that each factor is coprime to the product of the preceding ones, which is what the inductive argument uses.

results.what: If pairwise coprime numbers b, c, d each divide a, then their product bcd divides a. Proved by repeated use of Euclid's lemma: a = mb, c | m, so m = nc and a = nbc.
results.modern_name: Product of pairwise coprime divisors divides the number (corollary of Euclid's lemma / Gauss's lemma); basis of the CRT uniqueness part
results.usually_credited_to: Euclid (Elements VII), systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), art. 19

deep.surprise_reason: This is completely standard elementary number theory, found in Euclid and Gauss, written here as teaching-style notes. Nothing is new or attributable to Riemann as a result. The only curiosity is the bar notation 'a | b, c, d' for 'a divisible by b, c, d', which reads opposite to the modern convention and appears to be informal shorthand.

checkable.sympy: all(a % (b*c*d) == 0 for b,c,d in [(3,4,5),(7,9,10),(11,8,15)] for a in range(1,5000) if a%b==0 and a%c==0 and a%d==0)
checkable.asserts: For pairwise coprime b, c, d, divisibility of a by each implies divisibility by bcd (numerical check).

checkable.sympy: all(m % c == 0 for b,c in [(4,9),(5,7),(8,15)] for m in range(1,2000) if (m*b) % c == 0)
checkable.asserts: Step a = mb, c | a, gcd(b,c)=1 implies c | m (Euclid's lemma).

checkable.sympy: any(a % 4 == 0 and a % 6 == 0 and a % 24 != 0 for a in range(1,100))
checkable.asserts: The coprimality hypothesis is necessary: 12 is divisible by 4 and 6 but not by 24 (returns True).
A product of numbers each coprime to d is coprime to d, the fact needed for the final (implicit) step.

transcription_corrections: The final line appears to read 'a = nc·b' (written roughly as 'a = n c - b', possibly with a struck initial letter) rather than 'a = nbc'. The mathematical meaning is the same.
'welche sämmtlich relativ Primzahlen' is more likely 'welche sämmtlich relative Primzahlen', consistent with the previous page's usage.
The ruled line after the statement is 'a | b, c, d.' meaning 'a is divisible by b, c, d', not modern 'a divides b, c, d'.
